jurisdiction: European Union / EEA — horizontal digital law (EU-level instruments plus flagged member-state divergence). Excludes the gambling-licensing question, which is NOT harmonised at EU level and sits with 27 national regulators.
headline: CORRECTED HEADLINE. Under EU horizontal law the e-money cliff edge is THIRD-PARTY ACCEPTANCE AND TRANSFERABILITY, not redeemability. EMD2 (Directive 2009/110/EC) Art 2(2) has two cumulative limbs: (i) electronically stored monetary value representing a claim on the issuer, issued on receipt of funds for the purpose of making payment transactions, AND (ii) acceptance by a natural or legal person OTHER THAN the issuer. EBA Q&A 2022_6336 (Final, published 17/01/2025, citing CJEU C-661/22) reads limb (ii) as requiring 'the transferability and voluntary acceptance of electronic money as a separate monetary asset, and not simply as the reception by the payee of funds resulting from redeemed e-money'. A strictly closed-loop coin that only FACT//DUEL redeems, to the same customer who bought it, therefore FAILS limb (ii) however redeemable it is; redeemability is strong evidence of a payment purpose under limb (i), and redemption at par (Art 11) is an obligation that FOLLOWS from already being an issuer, not a trigger that creates one. What actually breaks the perimeter is player-to-player transferable value, an instrument third parties accept, or a priceable secondary market. Models A, C and D sit outside the e-money perimeter. Model B's real obstacles are (a) transferable / third-party-accepted value, (b) the money-OUT leg under PSD2, (c) AML obligations that are ALREADY LIVE today under national transpositions of AMLD4/AMLD5 — 10 July 2027 is when the AMLR replaces that regime, not when AML first bites — and (d) 27 national gambling regimes outside this lane. Every model that takes a euro carries TWO hard statutory obligations — destination-country VAT through non-Union OSS from the first euro (VAT Directive Arts 58, 73; no EUR 10,000 threshold because Art 59c is confined to EU-established sellers), and CRD Arts 6, 8(2) and 9 pre-contractual information, 'order with obligation to pay' button labelling and the 14-day withdrawal right — plus a THIRD, the Rome I Art 6 fact that the consumer's home mandatory law applies whatever your ToS says. The unspent-coin refund theory and the real-money price-labelling duty are NOT 'non-negotiable obligations': they rest wholly on the CPC Network Key Principles (21 March 2025), which expressly disclaim binding force. Treat them as declared enforcement posture, which is reason enough to build to them, but do not book them as law.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: MODEL A is lawful under every horizontal EU instrument in this lane, and the reason is cleaner than the original brief stated. (1) E-MONEY — CORRECTED. Coins are not electronic money because EMD2 Art 2(2) limb (ii) fails: only FACT//DUEL accepts them, no third party does, and they are not transferable as a separate monetary asset (EBA Q&A 2022_6336). Limb (i) also fails because they are not issued for the purpose of making payment transactions. The invariant to protect is NON-TRANSFERABILITY AND NO THIRD-PARTY ACCEPTANCE — no player-to-player gifting or trading, no priceable secondary market, no acceptance of your coin by any other merchant. The original brief told you that a goodwill cash refund or an account-closure balance return could make you an e-money issuer; the auditor is right that this is wrong, because a refund from you to your own customer involves no third party accepting anything. Consumer-friendly refunds are lawful and in fact partly mandatory. (2) VAT — CORRECTED AND STILL BINDING. A non-EU seller of a digital service to an EU consumer owes VAT at the consumer's member-state rate from the first euro: VAT Directive Art 58 (place of supply), Art 73 (taxable amount), and Art 59c's EUR 10,000 micro-threshold applies only to EU-ESTABLISHED sellers. That conclusion rests on the directive, NOT on CJEU C-472/24. C-472/24 MB 'Zaidimu valiuta' (judgment 5 March 2026) concerned a THIRD-PARTY TRADER reselling RuneScape gold on a secondary market, not a publisher issuing its own currency; the Court held that exchanging real currency for units usable only inside an online game is not exempt under Art 135(1)(e) and is not a voucher under Art 30a, so Art 73 general rules apply. Extending that to a first-party issuer's own coin sale is a reasonable inference, not a holding, and the single-purpose voucher analysis under Art 30a(2) for a first-party issuer was NOT before the Court. Take the conservative position (VAT at sale of coins) but know it is inference. (3) WITHDRAWAL — RE-LABELLED. CRD Art 9 gives a 14-day withdrawal right on the coin purchase contract. The CPC Network's further position — that in-game virtual currency is NOT itself digital content, so the Art 16(1)(m) waiver cannot extinguish that right, and unspent coins must be cash-refundable — is SOFT LAW that Video Games Europe and EGDF dispute and on which German courts have gone the other way (properly-run waivers upheld). Build the refund path because it is cheap and because it is the stated enforcement posture; do not describe it as settled law. (4) PRICING / UCPD — RE-LABELLED. Real-money price display at the undiscounted bundle rate, exact-amount coin purchase, no stacked currencies, and spending-off-by-default parental controls are CPC Key Principles positions built on UCPD Arts 5-9 and CRD Art 6(1)(e). The underlying UCPD misleading-omission analysis is real law; the specific prescriptions are the Network's reading of it. (5) AUDIT ADDITIONS. Directive (EU) 2019/770 (Digital Content Directive) is the core contract-law instrument here and was missing entirely: Arts 6-8 conformity, Arts 14-18 remedies and reimbursement on termination, and critically Art 19, which governs when you may MODIFY digital content or a digital service during continuous supply and gives the consumer a free termination right where a modification adversely affects access or use — that, not UCTD Art 3 alone, is what constrains post-launch coin rebalancing. CRD Art 8(2)'s 'order with obligation to pay' button labelling applies to EVERY coin-purchase button, not just a subscription confirm; non-compliance means the consumer is NOT BOUND by the contract, i.e. revenue reversal. Directive 2000/31/EC Arts 5, 6 and 10 impose provider-identification and commercial-communication duties alongside CRD Art 6, and its Art 3 country-of-origin principle gives a non-EU-established provider nothing. Rome I Regulation (EC) 593/2008 Art 6(1)-(2) is why all of this binds you at all: a trader directing activities to a member state is subject to the mandatory consumer-protection law of the consumer's habitual residence, and a choice-of-law clause cannot take it away; Brussels Ia Regulation (EU) 1215/2012 Art 18 lets the consumer sue at home. None of this makes Model A unlawful; all of it makes an unmodified launch unlawful.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: MODEL B breaks the horizontal perimeter, but for corrected reasons. (1) E-MONEY — CORRECTED. The question is NOT 'is the balance redeemable'. It is whether EMD2 Art 2(2) limb (ii) is satisfied: does someone other than the issuer accept the instrument, is it transferable, is it voluntarily accepted as a separate monetary asset (EBA Q&A 2022_6336, citing CJEU C-661/22)? In a dual-currency sweepstakes design the coins are staked PLAYER-VERSUS-PLAYER, which is exactly a transfer of stored value between persons other than the issuer, and winnings redeemable for cash or prizes of value supply the payment purpose under limb (i). That combination — not redeemability alone — is what makes Model B presumptively e-money issuance requiring EMI authorisation from a national competent authority (Central Bank of Ireland, BaFin, DNB, CSSF, MFSA and others), with initial capital, own-funds, safeguarding of client funds in segregated accounts, and passporting. A narrowly drafted operator-only redemption with NO player-to-player transfer might stay outside the definition; that is a perimeter question for counsel, not a founder. (2) PAYMENT SERVICES. Taking money from Player 1 into escrow and paying it to Player 2 looks like execution of payment transactions or money remittance (PSD2 Art 4(22), Annex I point 6). CJEU C-51/25 Betaal Garant Nederland (16 July 2026) narrowed this — transfers made only to deliver another, primary, non-payment service are not themselves a payment service, and a 'credit transfer' requires the intermediary to hold the payer's payment account — but commentators stress it is fact-specific and it expressly did NOT address money remittance. Holding named per-player balances is precisely what pushes you back inside. (3) AML — CORRECTED, AND THIS IS THE MOST DANGEROUS ERROR IN THE ORIGINAL BRIEF. AML obligations for gambling service providers are ALREADY LIVE across the EU under national transpositions of Directive (EU) 2015/849 (AMLD4, transposition deadline 26 June 2017) as amended by AMLD5. AMLD4 Art 3(14) already defines 'gambling services' in materially identical words to the AMLR — 'a service which involves wagering a stake with monetary value in games of chance, including those with an element of skill such as lotteries, casino games, poker games and betting transactions... provided at a physical location, or by any means at a distance, by electronic means... and at the individual request of a recipient of services' — and AMLD4 Art 2(1)(3)(f) has made providers of gambling services obliged entities EU-wide since 2017. The AMLR carries that wording into a regulation; it does not invent it. A Model B launch in 2026 with no AML programme would be unlawful in most member states ON DAY ONE. Comply with national AML law NOW; re-paper to Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) by 10 July 2027. CDD trigger for gambling: transactions of EUR 2,000 or more on collection of winnings, wagering of a stake, or both, single or linked (AMLD4 Art 11(d); carried into AMLR Art 19 — exact paragraph number UNVERIFIED). (4) PSD3/EMD2 REPEAL — AUDIT ADDITION, MATERIAL. PSD3 repeals EMD2 outright and merges the EMI and payment-institution regimes. Existing EMI authorisations survive only 24 months after entry into force (extendable to 30) with a MANDATORY RE-APPLICATION. An EMI licence obtained for Model B in 2027 would need re-papering almost immediately. (5) And then 27 national gambling regimes, outside this lane, where sweepstakes-casino structures have been the specific target of 2025-2026 enforcement. Verdict unchanged: not launchable in the EU without regulated-entity status or a licensed partner acting as merchant/issuer of record.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: MODEL C is the cleanest money-play structure under horizontal EU law but its characterisation is genuinely open, and the original brief overstated how much of it was settled. WHAT IS REASONABLY SETTLED: (a) if the entry fee is paid by card directly to you through an authorised PSP and the announced prize is paid out of your own treasury, you are not storing transferable third-party-accepted value, so EMD2 does not bite — this is the single design choice that keeps Model C outside e-money; (b) the CRD withdrawal right is manageable because a contest entry is a service the consumer expressly asks to begin immediately, and the Art 16(1)(a)/16(1)(m) waiver flow (separate click, explicit acknowledgement of loss of the right, Art 8(7) durable-medium confirmation) can be run properly; (c) after C-51/25 Betaal Garant a fixed prize paid from operator funds is a strong 'ancillary to the primary service' story for PSD2 purposes. WHAT IS NOT SETTLED — VAT, CORRECTED. The original brief called the VAT treatment of the entry fee 'settled' after testing it only against Art 135(1)(e) (currency transactions). The relevant provision is VAT Directive Art 135(1)(i), which exempts 'betting, lotteries and other forms of gambling, subject to the conditions and limitations laid down by each Member State'. If a member state characterises the paid-entry timed duel as gambling — precisely the question this brief calls unresolved for AML purposes — the entry fee may be VAT-EXEMPT in that state, outside the OSS return, with knock-on input-VAT recovery consequences. You cannot label the gambling characterisation 'unsettled' for AML and 'settled' for VAT when the same characterisation drives both. Related and also missing from the original: the Glawe line (C-38/93 Glawe; C-377/11 International Bingo Technology) can make the taxable amount for a wagering leg the OPERATOR'S RETAINED MARGIN rather than gross stakes. Both materially change the VAT model. WHAT IS NOT SETTLED — AML CHARACTERISATION. The 'games of chance, including those with an element of skill' wording has been EU law since AMLD4 Art 3(14) in 2015, not since the AMLR, so this exposure is PRESENT-TENSE, not a 2027 problem. A 5/7/10-second timed trivia duel over a randomly drawn question set is not obviously a pure skill contest: the question draw is stochastic and the timer converts knowledge into a probabilistic race. Whether such a contest is a gambling service (obliged entity, full CDD at EUR 2,000, FIU reporting) or a skill competition outside gambling entirely has no EU-level answer and no case law. THE ESCAPE HATCH THE ORIGINAL BRIEF OMITTED — AUDIT ADDITION. AMLD4 Art 2(2) expressly permits member states, other than for casinos and following a risk assessment, to 'exempt, in full or in part, providers of certain gambling services' from AML obligations on the basis of proven low risk, with notification to the Commission; the AML package preserves an equivalent low-risk exemption option. So whether a given paid-entry skill contest is an obliged entity remains a PER-MARKET answer both today and after 10 July 2027 — and this is the most plausible route for Model C. Ask, per market, whether the exemption has been exercised and whether your product falls in it. The fixed, pre-announced, entrant-count-independent prize pool remains the single most helpful fact — it removes the pooled-stake character most national regimes key on — but it does not resolve the statutory wording. Requires member-state counsel in each launch market; a favourable answer in one state is not portable.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: MODEL D is lawful under EU horizontal law and remains by a wide margin the lowest-risk monetisation for an EU launch: no stake, no prize, no stored transferable value, therefore no EMD2 perimeter question, no PSD2 issue beyond using an authorised PSP, no AML. What still applies: (1) VAT — a subscription supplied to an EU consumer is taxable at the consumer's rate under Art 58; a non-EU-established seller must register for non-Union OSS before the first sale, with no EUR 10,000 threshold (Art 59c is only for EU-established cross-border sellers). (2) CRD — Art 6 pre-contractual information, Art 8(2) 'order with obligation to pay' labelling on the confirm button, Art 9 14-day withdrawal on the initial subscription, and if you want immediate access the Art 16(1)(m) waiver must be run correctly: express consent plus acknowledgement of loss of the right in a click SEPARATE from the buy click, plus Art 8(7) durable-medium confirmation. (3) UCPD — cancellation must not be harder than sign-up; dark-pattern cancellation flows are the expected target of the forthcoming Digital Fairness Act. (4) Auto-renewal notice and easy-cancellation rules are set NATIONALLY, not by the CRD, and diverge sharply (Germany, France, Italy). (5) Do NOT include the old EU ODR-platform link in your terms: Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/3228 with effect from 20 July 2025 and the platform is switched off. ADR information duties under Directive 2013/11/EU survive. AUDIT ADDITIONS THAT LAND HARDEST ON A SUBSCRIPTION: Directive (EU) 2019/770 (DCD) Art 19 governs modification of a continuously-supplied digital service and gives the consumer a free termination right where a modification adversely affects access or use — this is the instrument that constrains changing what the subscription includes mid-term, and it was absent from the original brief; DCD Arts 14-18 govern conformity remedies, price reduction and reimbursement on termination, and the 'legal guarantee of conformity' you must disclose pre-contractually comes from here. Directive (EU) 2020/1828 on representative actions (applicable 25 June 2023) makes a subscription with a defective cancellation flow a collective-redress target, not just a regulator target. The European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) has APPLIED since 28 June 2025 to consumer-facing e-commerce services; you are exempt only while you are a microenterprise service provider (Art 4(5)) — under 10 staff and under EUR 2m turnover.
