checklist.item: Register for VAT non-Union OSS (or Union OSS if you incorporate in the EU) BEFORE the first EU coin/subscription sale
checklist.issuer: Tax authority of one chosen EU member state of identification (e.g. Irish Revenue, Dutch Belastingdienst); framework: Council Directive 2006/112/EC Arts 358a-369k
checklist.cost: No EU registration fee known; UNVERIFIED. Compliance-provider cost UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Legal entity; decide member state of identification
checklist.notes: CRITICAL AND ROUTINELY MISSED. [CORRECTED] The obligation follows from the VAT Directive itself, not from case law: Art 58 puts the place of supply of an electronically supplied service at the consumer's member state, Art 73 makes the taxable amount the full consideration, and the EUR 10,000 micro-threshold in Art 59c applies ONLY to EU-ESTABLISHED sellers — so a non-EU seller owes VAT from the first euro. CJEU C-472/24 MB 'Zaidimu valiuta' (5 March 2026) is supporting, not load-bearing, and is narrower than the original brief said: the taxable person was a THIRD-PARTY TRADER reselling RuneScape gold on a secondary market, not a publisher issuing its own currency. The Court held that exchanging real currency for units usable only inside an online game is not exempt under Art 135(1)(e) and is not a voucher under Art 30a, so Art 73 general rules apply. Extending that to a first-party issuer's own coin sale is a reasonable inference, NOT a holding; the single-purpose voucher analysis under Art 30a(2) for a first-party issuer was not before the Court. Take the conservative position (VAT at the coin sale, on full consideration) and document it as an inference. Displayed coin prices must be VAT-inclusive for consumers and the rate varies by member state — see the geo-blocking checklist item before varying price per country.

checklist.item: Collect and store two pieces of non-contradictory customer-location evidence for every EU sale
checklist.issuer: Council Implementing Regulation (EU) No 282/2011 Arts 24b, 24f
checklist.prerequisite: OSS registration
checklist.notes: Billing address, IP geolocation, card BIN country, SIM country. Retain 10 years. Your product is currently accountless and stores everything in IndexedDB — that gives you NO location evidence, so this is a real backend requirement, not paperwork.

checklist.item: Appoint a GDPR Article 27 EU representative in writing
checklist.issuer: Private appointment; details must be published and given to data subjects and supervisory authorities (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Arts 13(1)(a), 14(1)(a), 27)
checklist.prerequisite: Confirm you have no EU establishment; identify a member state where your data subjects are
checklist.notes: Mandatory for any non-EU controller offering services to people in the EU (Art 3(2)(a)). The Art 27(2)(a) 'occasional processing' exemption is cumulative and effectively unavailable to a live consumer game that processes continuously. Appoint in a member state where a substantial share of your players are. SEPARATE from the DSA legal representative below — do not conflate them, though one vendor can often supply both.

checklist.item: Designate a DSA Article 13 legal representative and notify the Digital Services Coordinator
checklist.issuer: Digital Services Coordinator of the member state of designation; framework: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA) Art 13 — DSA fully applicable 17 Feb 2024
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — only if you are an 'intermediary service' (see notes)
checklist.prerequisite: Scoping decision on whether you are a hosting service
checklist.notes: SCOPE FIRST, THEN APPOINT. Today FACT//DUEL is almost certainly outside the DSA: all state is local, there is no storage of user-provided information. The moment you add accounts you will store player-chosen display names, duel room codes and any chat — that is 'storage of information provided by a recipient', i.e. a HOSTING service under DSA Art 3(g)(iii), which triggers Arts 11, 12, 14 and 16 including the Art 13 representative (who can be held personally liable for your non-compliance). You are very likely NOT an 'online platform' under Art 3(i), because a 1v1 duel is not 'dissemination to the public' — interpersonal 1:1 communication is expressly outside. Consequence: the Section 3 duties (Arts 20-28, including Art 28 minor protection) do not apply, and Art 19 exempts micro/small enterprises from Section 3 anyway. If you ever add public leaderboards with user-authored text, global chat, or user-generated question packs, you become an online platform and this analysis flips.

checklist.item: Complete a GDPR Article 35 Data Protection Impact Assessment before launching accounts or real-money play
checklist.issuer: Self-assessed; consult the lead supervisory authority under Art 36 if high residual risk. Each DPA publishes an Art 35(4) mandatory-DPIA list
checklist.prerequisite: Records of processing (Art 30); data map
checklist.notes: A DPIA is effectively unavoidable here. National Art 35(4) lists commonly mandate a DPIA for services likely to be accessed by children and for profiling/behavioural tracking. You have: a knowledge game likely to appeal to minors, session/retention analytics, skill-based matchmaking, streak and spend mechanics. If Model B or C, add financial data and gambling-adjacent behavioural risk, which pushes it firmly into Art 35(3)(a).

checklist.item: Maintain Article 30 records of processing activities (ROPA)
checklist.issuer: Self-maintained; producible to any supervisory authority on request
checklist.prerequisite: Data map
checklist.notes: The Art 30(5) sub-250-employee carve-out is cumulative and does not apply: your processing is neither occasional nor risk-free. As a non-EU controller the ROPA must also be kept by your Art 27 representative.

checklist.item: Run a documented DPO-necessity assessment under Article 37(1)(b)-(c)
checklist.issuer: Self-assessed; if appointed, notify the supervisory authority (Art 37(7))
checklist.prerequisite: Scale estimate of monitoring
checklist.notes: The 250-employee number is in Art 30 only and has nothing to do with DPOs. The trigger is 'core activities' consisting of 'regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale'. A retention/cohort analytics engine plus matchmaking plus spend telemetry across a consumer player base is exactly the fact pattern regulators treat as regular and systematic monitoring. Write the assessment down even if the answer is no.

checklist.item: Map a lawful basis to every processing purpose and stop relying on a single blanket consent
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art 6
checklist.prerequisite: Data map
checklist.notes: Art 6(1)(b) contract for account, duel delivery, coin ledger and payment; Art 6(1)(c) legal obligation for VAT records and (in Model B/C) AML records — note AML record-keeping is a legal obligation TODAY under national AMLD4/5 law, not from 2027; Art 6(1)(f) legitimate interests for anti-cheat, collusion detection and fraud prevention (do a documented LIA); Art 6(1)(a) consent for analytics, marketing and any personalised offer. The existing opt-in cohort ping in lib/cohort-client.ts is already built consent-gated, which is the right shape — keep that discipline.

checklist.item: Implement ePrivacy consent for non-essential terminal-equipment storage
checklist.issuer: National implementations of Directive 2002/58/EC Art 5(3) (e.g. CNIL in France, Garante in Italy, DSK guidance in Germany)
checklist.prerequisite: Inventory of IndexedDB/localStorage keys
checklist.notes: Art 5(3) covers ANY storing of or access to information on the user's device, not just cookies — your IndexedDB profile store is in scope. Game-state persistence needed to deliver the service the user asked for is strictly-necessary and exempt; the analytics day-rows and anonId are not, and need prior consent. ePrivacy is a directive, so this is 27 slightly different rules; the German TDDDG and the French CNIL guidance are the strictest in practice.

checklist.item: Decide international-transfer mechanism for every US or non-EEA processor
checklist.issuer: European Commission adequacy decision of 10 July 2023 (EU-US DPF); or Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 SCCs
checklist.cost: DPF self-certification fee to US Dept of Commerce: UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Vendor inventory (Cloudflare, Stripe, analytics, error tracking)
checklist.notes: STATUS AS AT SEPT 2026: the DPF is still valid. The General Court dismissed the annulment action in Latombe v Commission (Case T-553/23) on 3 September 2025; Latombe appealed on 31 October 2025 and the appeal is pending before the Court of Justice as Case C-703/25 P, limited to points of law. [CORRECTED] The case number C-703/25 P is corroborated by independent secondary sources (EDPL 2026/1; practitioner commentary) and is retained. The original brief's further claims — 'no hearing date announced as at mid-2026' and 'Microsoft granted leave to intervene for the Commission on 29 June 2026' — are UNCORROBORATED and have been REMOVED; do not repeat them without checking the CURIA register. The CJEU killed both predecessor frameworks, so DO NOT build a US-processor stack that only works if the DPF survives. Put SCCs plus a transfer impact assessment in place as a fallback in every US processor contract now.

checklist.item: Show the real-money price alongside every coin price, at the undiscounted rate
checklist.issuer: CPC Network (national consumer authorities coordinated by the European Commission), Key Principles on In-game Virtual Currencies, 21 March 2025 — Principles 1 and 2 — SOFT LAW
checklist.prerequisite: Coin-to-euro reference rate per member state
checklist.notes: [RE-LABELLED — ENFORCEMENT POSTURE, NOT A STATUTORY OBLIGATION]. Legal basis the CPC Network cites: UCPD Arts 6(1)(d) and 7, CRD Art 6(1)(e). The underlying misleading-omission analysis is real law; the specific prescription is the Network's reading of it, and the Key Principles expressly state they do not bind national authorities or the Commission and that non-compliance is not necessarily unlawful. Video Games Europe and EGDF have publicly disputed parts of the document. Build to it anyway — it is the declared posture of the authorities who would open the file, and a live CPC coordinated action against Star Stable Entertainment AB was announced the same day. The stated rule: the price must be the objective cost of buying the required coins IN FULL, without quantity discounts or promos, regardless of how the player actually obtained the coins. Principle 2 also says do not run several stacked currencies or force multi-step currency exchanges. Your current 0/10/25/50/100 stake ladder and Expedition POINTS tier are fine today, but the instant coins are purchasable you must not let points and coins interconvert in a way that obscures the euro cost.

checklist.item: Let players buy the exact amount of coins they need; never force an over-purchase bundle
checklist.issuer: CPC Network Key Principles, Principle 3 (legal basis asserted: UCPD Arts 5, 8, 9) — SOFT LAW
checklist.prerequisite: Coin shop design
checklist.notes: [RE-LABELLED — ENFORCEMENT POSTURE]. The two named practices to avoid are (i) offering coins only in bundles that mismatch the price of purchasable content, and (ii) denying the player the ability to choose the amount. This is the single most common design pattern in the market and the CPC Network has singled it out as likely to distort economic behaviour. Design your shop with an arbitrary-amount option from day one — retrofitting it after launch is far more expensive than building it.

checklist.item: Build a 14-day withdrawal and refund flow, and decide your position on UNSPENT coins
checklist.issuer: Directive 2011/83/EU Arts 9-16 (STATUTORY); CPC Network Key Principles, Principle 5 (SOFT LAW, contested)
checklist.prerequisite: Coin ledger that distinguishes spent from unspent balance
checklist.notes: [SPLIT INTO HARD AND SOFT]. HARD LAW: CRD Art 9 gives a 14-day withdrawal right on a distance contract, and CRD Art 16(1)(m) lets you extinguish it for digital content only if you run consent + acknowledgement of loss of the right in a click SEPARATE from the buy button and send an Art 8(7) durable-medium confirmation. SOFT AND CONTESTED: the CPC Network's further position is that in-game virtual currency is NOT itself digital content, so the Art 16(1)(m) waiver cannot cover the coin purchase and unspent coins must be cash-refundable within 14 days. Named practices to avoid: 'exempting the purchase of in-game virtual currency, which is not digital content, from the right of withdrawal' and 'denying consumers' right to withdraw... for any in-game virtual currency that remains unused'. This premise is a CPC legal theory that Video Games Europe/EGDF dispute and on which GERMAN COURTS HAVE GONE THE OTHER WAY, upholding properly-constructed waivers for virtual currency. Practical build: track FIFO coin lots with purchase timestamps and refund the unspent remainder of any lot younger than 14 days. Cheaper than litigating it. Do not record it as settled law.

checklist.item: Rewrite terms of service to remove unfair terms flagged by the CPC Network, and to comply with DCD Art 19 on modifications
checklist.issuer: CPC Network Key Principles, Principle 6 (asserted basis: UCTD Directive 93/13/EEC Art 3(1) and (3)) — SOFT LAW; PLUS Directive (EU) 2019/770 (DCD) Art 19 — HARD LAW [AUDIT ADDITION]
checklist.prerequisite: Draft ToS
checklist.notes: [CORRECTED — the binding constraint on post-launch coin rebalancing is DCD Art 19, which the original brief never cited]. DCD Art 19 governs when a trader may MODIFY digital content or a digital service during a period of continuous supply: the contract must allow it, there must be a valid reason, it must be at no additional cost, the consumer must be informed in advance on a durable medium, and where the modification adversely affects access to or use of the content the consumer gets a FREE TERMINATION RIGHT (with DCD Arts 16-18 reimbursement). DCD Arts 6-8 set conformity and Arts 14-18 the remedies; the 'legal guarantee of conformity' that CPC Principle 4 requires you to disclose pre-contractually comes from this directive. SEPARATELY, CPC Principle 6 names as terms to avoid: unilateral rights to cease/modify/withdraw purchased content or purchased virtual currency; terms denying or limiting statutory rights; unilateral removal of purchasable features players expected to persist; A UNILATERAL RIGHT TO CHANGE THE VALUE OF THE VIRTUAL CURRENCY; and banning/suspending accounts or confiscating purchased content with no way to contest. Design the economy knowing you cannot silently devalue coins people paid for. Also: DELETE any EU ODR-platform link from your template terms — Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/3228 effective 20 July 2025 and the platform is switched off. ADR disclosure duties under Directive 2013/11/EU survive.

checklist.item: Turn real-money spending OFF by default and ship functional parental controls
checklist.issuer: CPC Network Key Principles, Principle 7 (asserted basis: UCPD Arts 5-8 and Annex I point 28) — SOFT LAW, but Annex I point 28 is hard law
checklist.prerequisite: Account system
checklist.notes: The CPC Network's explicit action point: 'by default disabling the possibility of spending real-world money in the video game if the video game is not exclusively limited to an adult audience'. It also says ANY game not exclusively intended for adults should expect a significant under-18 player base, and that age gates do NOT discharge your responsibility. Two stings that bite this product hard: UCPD Annex I point 28 is a BLACKLISTED practice in the directive itself (direct exhortations to children to buy) and needs no CPC theory to be unlawful; and the guidance treats high-spending 'whales' as themselves a VULNERABLE group likely to struggle with impulse control or gambling disorders, so a business model built on whale extraction is assessed against a stricter fairness threshold. FACT//DUEL's juice/streak/escrow loop is precisely the design vocabulary this principle is aimed at.

checklist.item: Choose and document an age-assurance method proportionate to the model
checklist.issuer: EDPB Statement 1/2025 on Age Assurance (adopted Feb 2025); European Commission age-verification blueprint / 'mini-wallet'; Commission Guidelines on the protection of minors under DSA Art 28 (July 2025)
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — proportionate to risk; strictest for B and C
checklist.prerequisite: DPIA; decision on whether you are an 'online platform' under DSA Art 3(i)
checklist.notes: [CORRECTED STATUS OF THE BLUEPRINT]. Version 1 of the Commission's age-verification blueprint was published 14 July 2025 and the five pilot member states (Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Spain) are confirmed. The original brief's claim that the Commission 'declared the blueprint feature-ready on 15 April 2026' is UNTRACEABLE and has been REMOVED. What is documented: the Commission released an ENHANCED SECOND VERSION on 10 October 2025, describing the blueprint as 'now being thoroughly pilot tested' and saying 'the first customised apps are expected to be published early 2026'; no 'feature-ready' declaration exists in any reachable source. Current readiness as at Sept 2026: UNVERIFIED. Substance unchanged: the EDPB's ten principles require the LEAST intrusive effective method against five criteria — accuracy, reliability, robustness, non-intrusiveness, non-discrimination — and distinguish self-declaration, age estimation and age verification. Self-declaration is defensible for Model A/D; it is not defensible for Model B and is doubtful for Model C. Integrating against the EUDI Wallet specs is the strategically correct bet, but adopting the app is not itself a compliance discharge. Separately, GDPR Art 8 sets the age of consent for information-society services at a default of 16 with member states free to lower it to 13 — the parental-consent age literally changes at the border (see subdivisions).

checklist.item: Contract an authorised PSP as merchant of record / acquirer and implement SCA
checklist.issuer: PSP authorised under Directive (EU) 2015/2366; SCA under PSD2 Art 97 and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389
checklist.prerequisite: Legal entity, bank account, KYB onboarding with the PSP
checklist.notes: [PSD3 STATUS CORRECTED]. Using an authorised PSP is how you stay OUT of the PSD2 perimeter for the money-in leg. Implement EMV 3DS2 and handle the soft-decline/step-up path or your EU conversion collapses. A merchant-of-record PSP can also carry the VAT/OSS burden — worth pricing against doing OSS yourself. PSD3/PSR STATUS: provisional political agreement 27 November 2025 is corroborated. The original brief's '23 April 2026 final compromise texts' date appears in NO reachable source and has been REMOVED. The brief's own cited source (Norton Rose Fulbright) puts expected OJ publication at END OF Q2 2026 (not 'H2 2026') and the PSR application at 18 MONTHS after entry into force (not ~21), with only the payee-name/identifier verification duty at 24 months. Whether OJ publication has in fact occurred as at Sept 2026: UNVERIFIED. PSD2 and the 2018/389 RTS remain the operative law you should build to. MATERIAL ADDITION: PSD3 REPEALS EMD2 OUTRIGHT and merges the EMI and payment-institution regimes; existing EMI authorisations survive only 24 months after entry into force (extendable to 30) with a MANDATORY RE-APPLICATION.

checklist.item: Obtain a regulatory perimeter opinion on whether holding player balances makes you a payment institution or an EMI
checklist.issuer: National competent authority (e.g. Central Bank of Ireland, BaFin, DNB, CSSF, MFSA) — via counsel
checklist.appliesTo: B mandatory; C strongly recommended; A only if you ever add coin transferability or third-party acceptance
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec including the exact money-in and money-out flows
checklist.notes: THE DECISION POINT OF THIS WHOLE ANALYSIS. [CORRECTED TEST]. Two limbs of EMD2 Art 2(2) must BOTH be satisfied: (i) electronically stored monetary value representing a claim on the issuer, issued on receipt of funds for the purpose of making payment transactions, AND (ii) accepted by a natural or legal person OTHER THAN the issuer. EBA Q&A 2022_6336 (Final, 17/01/2025, citing CJEU C-661/22) says limb (ii) requires 'the transferability and voluntary acceptance of electronic money as a separate monetary asset, and not simply as the reception by the payee of funds resulting from redeemed e-money'. CONSEQUENCE: coins that only you accept, that no one else accepts, and that players cannot transfer are NOT e-money — even if you redeem them yourself. Redeemability is evidence of a payment purpose under limb (i), not a standalone trigger; Art 11 redemption at par is an obligation that follows from already being an issuer. What genuinely engages limb (ii): player-to-player staking or gifting, transferable balances, acceptance by any third-party merchant, a priceable grey market. For the money-OUT leg, CJEU C-51/25 Betaal Garant Nederland (16 July 2026) helps: fund transfers made only to deliver a primary non-payment service are not themselves a payment service, and a credit transfer requires the intermediary to hold the payer's payment account. But the Court expressly did not address MONEY REMITTANCE (PSD2 Art 4(22), Annex I point 6), practitioners call the ruling fact-specific, and two further CJEU references are pending. Do not lean on Betaal Garant as a licence substitute. Instruct counsel on the PSD3 transition too: an EMI licence granted in 2027 requires re-application within 24-30 months.

checklist.item: If any payment instrument you issue is used within a limited network, notify at the EUR 1 million threshold
checklist.issuer: National competent authority; PSD2 Art 37(2); EBA Guidelines EBA/GL/2022/02 on the limited network exclusion, applicable 1 June 2022
checklist.prerequisite: Transaction volume monitoring instrumented in the coin ledger
checklist.notes: If you rely on the PSD2 Art 3(k) limited-network exclusion, Art 37(2) requires a notification to your competent authority when the total value of payment transactions over any period shorter than 12 months exceeds EUR 1,000,000. The EBA guidelines say the notification is filed once, with a fresh one if the information changes substantially. Instrument your coin ledger to measure this from day one — a threshold you cannot measure is a threshold you will breach silently.

checklist.item: Stand up AML/CFT capability NOW under national AMLD4/AMLD5 law if you pursue Model B or C — then re-paper to the AMLR by 10 July 2027
checklist.issuer: National AML supervisors and FIUs under national transpositions of Directive (EU) 2015/849 as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/843 — IN FORCE SINCE 26 June 2017; from 10 July 2027, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) applies directly, supervised by national supervisors and the new Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA)
checklist.appliesTo: B mandatory TODAY; C to be determined per member state, TODAY
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — but must precede launch, not follow it
checklist.prerequisite: Identity verification, transaction monitoring, record-keeping infrastructure, and a per-market answer on whether you are an obliged entity
checklist.notes: [CORRECTED — THIS WAS THE MOST DANGEROUS ITEM IN THE ORIGINAL BRIEF, WHICH GAVE A 2027 START DATE]. AML obligations for gambling service providers are ALREADY LIVE across the EU. AMLD4 Art 2(1)(3)(f) has made 'providers of gambling services' obliged entities EU-wide since the 26 June 2017 transposition deadline, and AMLD4 Art 3(14) already defines gambling services in materially identical words to the AMLR: 'a service which involves wagering a stake with monetary value in games of chance, including those with an element of skill such as lotteries, casino games, poker games and betting transactions that are provided at a physical location, or by any means at a distance, by electronic means or any other technology for facilitating communication, and at the individual request of a recipient of services'. So the AMLR did NOT give the first EU-wide definition and 10 July 2027 is NOT the date AML first bites — it is the date a directly-applicable regulation replaces the national regime. Launching Model B in late 2026 with no AML programme would be unlawful in most member states on day one. Live obligations: customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, FIU suspicious-transaction reporting, record-keeping, and registration/licensing with the national AML supervisor. CDD TRIGGER [audit addition, now researched]: transactions of EUR 2,000 or more, on collection of winnings, wagering of a stake, or both, in a single operation or several linked operations — AMLD4 Art 11(d), carried into AMLR Art 19 (exact AMLR paragraph number UNVERIFIED); the AMLR also expects monitoring BELOW the threshold to catch structuring. Whether Model C's paid-entry contest is inside 'games of chance... including those with an element of skill' is unresolved and needs counsel per market — see the low-risk-exemption item below.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Check, per launch market, whether the national low-risk exemption for certain gambling services has been exercised and whether you fall in it
checklist.issuer: National AML supervisor / ministry; Directive (EU) 2015/849 (AMLD4) Art 2(2), with notification to the European Commission; equivalent low-risk exemption option preserved in the AML package
checklist.appliesTo: C primarily; B unlikely to qualify
checklist.prerequisite: Per-market characterisation opinion; documented risk assessment of your product
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION — the original brief said the AMLR ends forum-shopping of the definition, which OVERSTATES uniformity]. AMLD4 Art 2(2) expressly permits member states, OTHER THAN FOR CASINOS and following an appropriate risk assessment, to 'exempt, in full or in part, providers of certain gambling services' from AML obligations on the basis of proven low risk, with notification to the Commission; the AML package preserves an equivalent option. Consequence: whether a given paid-entry skill contest is an AML obliged entity remains a PER-MARKET answer both today and after 10 July 2027. This is the most plausible escape hatch for Model C and the original brief omitted it entirely. Action: for each launch market, establish (a) has the state exercised the Art 2(2) exemption, (b) for which categories of gambling service, (c) does a fixed-prize paid-entry trivia contest fall within the exempted category, (d) what risk assessment or notification is needed from you. Do not assume portability between states.

checklist.item: Document a DAC7 scoping conclusion (likely out of scope) and keep it on file
checklist.issuer: Council Directive (EU) 2021/514 (DAC7), amending Directive 2011/16/EU; reporting to the tax authority of the member state of registration
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — assess, probably not report
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec
checklist.notes: DAC7's four 'Relevant Activities' are exhaustive: rental of immovable property, personal services, sale of (tangible) goods, and rental of any mode of transport. Prize money and gaming winnings are not among them, and players in a duel are not 'Sellers' providing a personal service to a customer for consideration. So on the current design, none of Models A-D triggers DAC7 reporting. WRITE THE CONCLUSION DOWN. It would change if you ever add a creator marketplace (user-authored question packs sold to other players), paid coaching, or any revenue-share payout to individual content providers — at which point you become a reporting platform operator with annual reporting. Confirm with a tax adviser against your chosen member state's implementation; there is no Commission guidance specifically addressing gaming prizes. Annex V Section I(A)(8) not read directly — UNVERIFIED.

checklist.item: Confirm the AI Act does not apply, and re-test the conclusion if you add any AI
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act); national market surveillance authorities and the EU AI Office
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — currently not applicable
checklist.prerequisite: Code audit of the deployed build
checklist.notes: Repository check: there is no LLM or AI dependency in the shipped product (no OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini or ML inference in app/, lib/ or components/). The AI Act therefore does not currently apply. TWO TRIGGERS TO WATCH. First, if you add AI-driven personalised offers, dynamic difficulty tuned to spending, or emotion/behaviour inference aimed at maximising stake size, test against the Art 5 PROHIBITED practices — Art 5(1)(a) manipulative or deceptive techniques materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm, and Art 5(1)(b) exploitation of vulnerabilities including age — in force since 2 February 2025, highest fine tier. A gambling-adjacent product with whale-targeted personalisation is close to that line. Second, if you add AI-generated questions or a chatbot, Art 50 transparency duties apply — and these remain LIVE from 2 August 2026; they were not deferred. [CONTESTED — do not rely on these dates]: the original brief stated the AI Omnibus 'was adopted by Council 29 June 2026, published in the OJ 24 July 2026 and entered into force 27 July 2026'. The brief's own cited source records only political agreement 6 May 2026, Council confirmation 13 May 2026, and formal adoption plus OJ publication 'expected before 2 August 2026'. No reachable source corroborates the 29 June / 24 July / 27 July chain and a three-day OJ-to-entry-into-force interval is atypical. TREAT THESE DATES AS CONTESTED AND UNVERIFIED; verify the OJ citation before relying on any deferral. The SUBSTANCE does check out: stand-alone Annex III high-risk obligations deferred to 2 December 2027, Annex I embedded high-risk to 2 August 2028, Art 5 prohibitions NOT deferred. Also: a new Art 5 prohibition (nudifiers/CSAM) was added with a transitional period to 2 December 2026 [AUDIT ADDITION].

checklist.item: Confirm MiCA does not apply
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 (MiCA); ESMA/EBA and national competent authorities
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — not applicable on current design
checklist.prerequisite: Confirm no DLT or blockchain in the coin ledger
checklist.notes: MiCA's crypto-asset definition turns on the value being transferable and stored using distributed ledger technology or similar technology. A centrally-ledgered coin balance in your own database is not a crypto-asset and MiCA does not apply. Exact article reference and any in-game carve-out recital: UNVERIFIED. This conclusion breaks immediately if anyone proposes putting coins on-chain or making them tradeable — at which point you would face BOTH MiCA and (for a redeemable, transferable coin) the e-money-token regime, which is the worst of all worlds. Note the overlap with the corrected EMD2 test: on-chain tradeability is precisely what satisfies EMD2 Art 2(2) limb (ii).

checklist.item: Ship DSA baseline compliance if and when you become a hosting service
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA) Arts 11, 12, 14, 16 (NOT Art 15 — see notes); supervised by the Digital Services Coordinator of your member state of establishment or of your legal representative
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — only once accounts introduce stored user-provided information
checklist.prerequisite: Art 13 legal representative designated; DSA scoping decision made
checklist.notes: [CORRECTED — ART 15 REMOVED]. Baseline duties that apply regardless of Section 3 exemptions: Art 11 single point of contact for authorities, Art 12 point of contact for users, Art 14 terms and conditions written clearly including your content-restriction policies, and — for hosting services — Art 16 notice-and-action mechanisms for illegal content. ART 15 TRANSPARENCY REPORTING DOES NOT APPLY TO YOU: Art 15(2) provides that Art 15(1) 'shall not apply to providers of intermediary services that qualify as micro or small enterprises as defined in Recommendation 2003/361/EC and which are not very large online platforms within the meaning of Article 33'. This brief assumes micro/small status elsewhere (it relies on Art 19 for exactly that), so listing Art 15 among size-blind baseline duties was a misstatement that would have generated unnecessary annual reporting work. Because you are very likely not an 'online platform' (no dissemination to the public), Arts 20-28 do not apply, and Art 19 would exempt you from Section 3 anyway as a micro/small enterprise, with a 12-month grace period after you outgrow that status. Re-run this scoping if you add public chat, global leaderboards with user text, or user-generated question packs.

checklist.item: Track the Digital Fairness Act and design to its expected requirements now
checklist.issuer: European Commission (proposal expected H2 2026); NOT YET LAW
checklist.leadTime: Adoption unlikely before 2027; application later — all timing UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Coin economy design decisions not yet locked
checklist.notes: COMMENTARY AND TRADE PRESS, NOT LAW. The DFA is trailed as a single instrument covering dark patterns, addictive design, loot boxes, virtual currencies, influencer marketing and unfair personalised pricing. Two expected provisions land directly on this product: an obligation to display the real-world monetary value of in-game purchasable items even when priced in virtual currency (which the CPC Key Principles already assert as current law — itself contested), and possibly an outright loot-box ban or a parental-consent requirement for minors, with the Netherlands reported to be pushing for a full ban. Practical advice: if you build the real-money price display and the exact-amount coin purchase now, DFA compliance is close to free later; if you build a stacked dual-currency economy with randomised paid rewards, you are building a product you may have to dismantle. Treat every timeline claim here as unconfirmed press reporting.

checklist.item: Obtain member-state gambling counsel in every launch market before Model B or C
checklist.issuer: National gambling regulators (out of this lane)
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec including stake mechanics and prize determination
checklist.notes: There is no EU gambling directive. Gambling is reserved to member states subject only to the TFEU free-movement rules (Arts 49 and 56) as policed by the CJEU, which permits national restrictions on public-interest grounds. That means 27 separate answers on whether a timed trivia duel for money is gambling, a skill competition, or a prize contest — and a favourable answer in Malta tells you nothing about Germany, the Netherlands or Poland. Horizontal EU law CANNOT resolve this. Instruct the SAME counsel on three linked questions at once, because one characterisation drives all three: gambling licensing, AML obliged-entity status (live today, not 2027), and VAT Art 135(1)(i) exemption.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Comply with Directive (EU) 2019/770 (Digital Content Directive) across conformity, modification and termination
checklist.issuer: Directive (EU) 2019/770 — transposition 1 July 2021, applicable to contracts from 1 January 2022; enforced through national contract law and national consumer authorities
checklist.prerequisite: Draft ToS; product spec for coins, cosmetics and any subscription
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION — the single largest gap in the original brief's consumer-law layer: the DCD was never cited once]. This is the core contract-law instrument for exactly this product. Arts 6-8: objective and subjective conformity requirements for digital content and digital services. Arts 14-18: remedies for non-conformity, price reduction, and reimbursement on termination. ART 19 IS THE ONE THAT CONSTRAINS YOUR ECONOMY: it governs when a trader may modify digital content or a digital service during continuous supply — permitted only where the contract allows it, there is a valid reason, it is at no extra cost, and the consumer is informed in advance on a durable medium; and where the modification ADVERSELY AFFECTS ACCESS TO OR USE of the content, the consumer gets a free termination right. This, not UCTD Art 3 alone, is the hard-law limit on post-launch coin rebalancing, cosmetic removal and feature withdrawal. The 'legal guarantee of conformity for digital content and services' that CPC Principle 4 requires you to disclose pre-contractually comes from here. Get your ToS drafted against the DCD, not just against a US-style EULA template.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Scope the European Accessibility Act and set a trigger alarm at the microenterprise threshold
checklist.issuer: Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) — requirements APPLY SINCE 28 June 2025; enforced by national market surveillance authorities with fines
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — exempt today only as a microenterprise service provider
checklist.leadTime: Months if retrofitted — design it in instead
checklist.prerequisite: Headcount and turnover tracking; accessibility audit of the app shell
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION — not mentioned once in the original brief]. The EAA expressly covers e-commerce and consumer-facing digital services, i.e. websites and mobile apps used to conclude consumer contracts — which is exactly what a coin shop or subscription checkout is. Art 4(5) exempts MICROENTERPRISES providing services, which is why you can ignore it today. The exemption evaporates at 10 staff or EUR 2m annual turnover. Retrofitting WCAG-level accessibility into a heavily animated, timer-driven, juice-and-ceremony game UI after launch is expensive: timed inputs, motion, colour-coded answer shapes and audio-cued ceremonies are all EAA-relevant. FACT//DUEL already has reduced-motion support, which is the right direction. Action: put a headcount/turnover trigger in the compliance calendar, and build the checkout flow to accessibility standards from day one even while exempt.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Fix the governing-law and jurisdiction clauses: a US or offshore choice of law does NOT displace EU consumer protection
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EC) No 593/2008 (Rome I) Art 6(1)-(2); Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 (Brussels Ia) Arts 17-19
checklist.prerequisite: Draft ToS
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION — the original brief asserted throughout that the CRD, UCPD, UCTD and DCD bind a non-EU trader without ever explaining why]. Rome I Art 6(1) applies the law of the consumer's habitual residence to a contract with a trader who 'by any means, directs' commercial activities to that member state; Art 6(2) permits a choice of law but provides that it 'may not... have the result of depriving the consumer of the protection afforded to him by provisions that cannot be derogated from by agreement' under that home law. Brussels Ia Art 18 lets the consumer sue in the courts of their own domicile and restricts where you can sue them. CONSEQUENCE: a US- or offshore-law ToS template does not solve the EU problem, and a founder handed one may believe it does. If you accept EUR pricing, localise, or market into the EU, you are 'directing activities'. Have the ToS reviewed on the assumption that 27 sets of mandatory consumer rules apply to the parts that cannot be contracted away.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Put a CRD Art 8(2) 'order with obligation to pay' button on EVERY purchase surface, not just the subscription confirm
checklist.issuer: Directive 2011/83/EU (CRD) Art 6 pre-contractual information and Art 8(2) confirm-button labelling; Art 8(7) durable-medium confirmation
checklist.prerequisite: Checkout design
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION — the original brief applied Art 8(2) only to Model D]. Art 8(2) requires that, for a distance contract concluded by electronic means placing the consumer under an obligation to pay, the trader make the consumer explicitly acknowledge that the order implies an obligation to pay, and that the order button be labelled unambiguously ('order with obligation to pay' or equivalent). THE SANCTION IS NOT A FINE: if you fail, the consumer is NOT BOUND BY THE CONTRACT. That is direct revenue reversal on every coin purchase, not a paperwork risk. It applies to every coin-purchase button in Models A, B and C exactly as it does to a subscription confirm. Pair it with Art 6 pre-contractual information on the same screen and Art 8(7) durable-medium confirmation after purchase.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Publish e-Commerce Directive provider identification and label commercial communications
checklist.issuer: Directive 2000/31/EC (e-Commerce Directive) Arts 5, 6 and 10, as implemented nationally
checklist.prerequisite: Legal entity details finalised
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION]. Baseline information-society-service provider duties that sit ALONGSIDE CRD Art 6 and apply independently of it: Art 5 requires easily, directly and permanently accessible identification — name, geographic address of establishment, contact details including email, trade/company register and registration number, and VAT identification number where applicable; Art 6 requires commercial communications to be clearly identifiable as such and to identify the person on whose behalf they are made, with promotional offers and their qualifying conditions clearly identifiable; Art 10 sets pre-order information duties for the technical steps of concluding a contract. Also note: the Art 3 COUNTRY-OF-ORIGIN principle offers a non-EU-established provider NOTHING — you get no single-market passport for your home-country rules, so the 27-market analysis stands.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Review per-country pricing against the Geo-blocking Regulation before implementing VAT-driven price variation
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2018/302 Art 4; enforced by national authorities designated under Art 7
checklist.prerequisite: Pricing decision; geolocation implementation
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION — the original brief advised 'either absorb the spread or vary the price per country' with no caveat]. Art 4 constrains applying different general conditions of access to an electronically supplied service for reasons related to a customer's nationality, place of residence or place of establishment. There IS room to price differently per market, but the IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL — how you determine the customer's country, whether you block or reroute, whether the difference is presented as a general condition of access — is exactly where geo-blocking complaints arise. Note the interaction with the OSS location-evidence item: the same geolocation signals that keep you VAT-compliant are the ones that can create a geo-blocking complaint if used to deny access rather than to set VAT. Get the design reviewed before you ship country-varying prices.

checklist.item: [AUDIT ADDITION] Take a documented position on the VAT gambling exemption and on the taxable amount for any wagering leg
checklist.issuer: Council Directive 2006/112/EC Art 135(1)(i); CJEU C-38/93 Glawe and CJEU C-377/11 International Bingo Technology; per-member-state conditions and limitations
checklist.appliesTo: B, C (and A only if any staking is added)
checklist.prerequisite: Per-market gambling characterisation opinion
checklist.notes: [AUDIT ADDITION — the original brief tested only Art 135(1)(e) and wrongly called Model C's VAT treatment 'settled']. Art 135(1)(i) exempts 'betting, lotteries and other forms of gambling, subject to the conditions and limitations laid down by each Member State'. If a member state characterises your paid-entry timed duel or your staked coin play as gambling, the entry fee or stake may be VAT-EXEMPT in that state and outside your OSS return — with knock-on input-VAT recovery consequences and a different cash-flow model. You cannot call the gambling characterisation unsettled for AML and settled for VAT: the same characterisation drives both. SEPARATELY, the Glawe line (C-38/93; C-377/11 International Bingo Technology) can make the taxable amount for a wagering supply the OPERATOR'S RETAINED MARGIN rather than gross stakes — a materially different VAT base for any Model B/C money-play variant. Both points must be settled per market with a tax adviser, and settled BEFORE you model revenue.

subdivisions.name: All 27 member states — GDPR Article 8 age of consent
subdivisions.detail: The age at which a child can consent to an information-society service without parental authorisation is set at 16 by default but member states may lower it to any age down to 13. This is not a uniform number: your parental-consent gate must be country-aware, and a single hardcoded age will be wrong somewhere. Note this only matters where CONSENT is your lawful basis — for contract-based processing (Art 6(1)(b)) the relevant question is national contractual capacity of minors, which also varies.

subdivisions.name: All 27 member states — gambling licensing
subdivisions.detail: Entirely outside harmonised EU law. Models B and C get a different answer in each state, and a licence or exemption in one confers nothing in another. Member-state counsel required per launch market. Out of this lane; flagged so it is not mistaken for a settled EU-level answer. [CORRECTED EMPHASIS] The same national characterisation also drives two things the original brief treated as EU-uniform: whether you are an AML obliged entity TODAY under national AMLD4/5 law, and whether the VAT Art 135(1)(i) gambling exemption applies. Instruct one counsel on all three.
subdivisions.authority: Arts 49 and 56 TFEU; CJEU case law on national gambling restrictions; no EU gambling directive exists

subdivisions.name: All 27 member states — ePrivacy Art 5(3) implementation
subdivisions.detail: Because ePrivacy is a directive, consent rules for storing/accessing information on the user's device (your IndexedDB analytics state, not the strictly-necessary game state) are implemented and enforced nationally, with material differences in what counts as valid consent and how aggressively it is policed. France (CNIL) and Germany (TDDDG, DSK guidance) are the practical high-water marks.
subdivisions.authority: Directive 2002/58/EC Art 5(3) as amended by Directive 2009/136/EC; national implementations

subdivisions.name: All 27 member states — subscription auto-renewal and cancellation (Model D)
subdivisions.detail: The CRD does not harmonise auto-renewal notice periods, maximum initial terms, or cancellation mechanics for ongoing subscriptions — these are national rules and they diverge materially, with Germany, France and Italy among the most prescriptive. Several states require a specific easy-cancellation mechanism. Exact national provisions NOT VERIFIED; obtain local counsel before launching Model D in any specific market. [AUDIT ADDITION] Note also that Directive (EU) 2019/770 Art 19 is EU-level hard law on MODIFYING a continuously-supplied digital service mid-term, and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 makes a defective cancellation flow a collective-redress target in any of these states.
subdivisions.authority: Directive 2011/83/EU does not cover this; national consumer statutes — specific sections UNVERIFIED. Directive (EU) 2019/770 Art 19; Directive (EU) 2020/1828

subdivisions.name: Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Spain — age-verification blueprint pilot
subdivisions.detail: [CORRECTED]. These five member states are the initial pilot for the Commission's age-verification 'mini-wallet', built on European Digital Identity Wallet technical specifications. Version 1 was published 14 July 2025 — CONFIRMED. The original brief's claim that 'the Commission declared the blueprint feature-ready on 15 April 2026' is UNTRACEABLE and has been REMOVED: no such declaration appears in any reachable source. What IS documented is an ENHANCED SECOND VERSION released 10 October 2025, which describes the blueprint as 'now being thoroughly pilot tested' and says 'the first customised apps are expected to be published early 2026'. Current readiness as at September 2026: UNVERIFIED. EUDI Wallet rollout was targeted before end-2026; status UNVERIFIED. If you need real age verification for Model B or C, these are the markets where a standards-based integration path exists first. Adopting the app is not itself a compliance discharge.
subdivisions.authority: European Commission age-verification blueprint (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu), v1 14 July 2025 and enhanced second version 10 October 2025; Commission Guidelines on protection of minors under DSA Art 28, July 2025

subdivisions.name: Sweden — CPC enforcement precedent
subdivisions.detail: The CPC Network's coordinated action announced alongside the Key Principles on 21 March 2025 targeted Star Stable Entertainment AB, a Swedish game operator, over direct exhortation to children in advertisements and time-limited pressure techniques in a virtual-currency economy. This is the live example of how the Key Principles are actually enforced — as a coordinated CPC action against a single operator, with commitments sought. Read it as the enforcement template for any coin economy aimed at or reaching minors. Note the enforcement value is independent of whether the Key Principles are binding: a CPC coordinated action is itself the punishment regardless of the eventual legal answer.
subdivisions.authority: CPC Network coordinated action, announced 21 March 2025 (European Commission news release)

subdivisions.name: Netherlands — loot box and virtual currency posture
subdivisions.detail: Reported (trade press, not law) as pushing for an explicit loot-box ban in the forthcoming Digital Fairness Act, consistent with its historically aggressive national stance on paid randomised rewards. If your roadmap ever includes randomised paid rewards, treat NL as the strictest market and design to it. This is commentary, not verified law.
subdivisions.authority: Secondary sources / trade press only — UNVERIFIED

subdivisions.name: Member state of identification for VAT OSS — a real choice
subdivisions.detail: A non-EU seller registering for non-Union OSS picks ONE member state to file through and reports all EU digital sales in a single return. The choice determines your filing language, portal, audit relationship and practical support quality, and is worth deliberating rather than defaulting. No physical presence in the EU is required for the non-Union scheme. Registration fees and lead times: UNVERIFIED. [AUDIT NOTE] The choice does NOT affect whether VAT is due — Art 58 puts the place of supply at the consumer's member state and Art 59c's EUR 10,000 threshold is confined to EU-established sellers, so a non-EU seller owes destination VAT from the first euro regardless of which state it files through.
subdivisions.authority: Council Directive 2006/112/EC Arts 358a-369k (non-Union scheme); Art 58 place of supply; Art 59c threshold (EU-established sellers only)

subdivisions.name: [AUDIT ADDITION] All 27 member states — AMLD4 Art 2(2) low-risk exemption for certain gambling services
subdivisions.detail: [AUDIT ADDITION — omitted entirely from the original brief, which claimed the AMLR ends forum-shopping of the gambling definition]. AMLD4 Art 2(2) permits member states, other than for casinos and following an appropriate risk assessment, to exempt in full or in part providers of certain gambling services from AML obligations on the basis of proven low risk, with notification to the European Commission; the AML package preserves an equivalent low-risk exemption option beyond 10 July 2027. Whether a fixed-prize, entrant-count-independent paid-entry skill contest sits inside a state's exempted category is therefore a PER-MARKET question both now and after the AMLR applies. This is the most plausible AML escape hatch for Model C. WHICH STATES HAVE EXERCISED IT, AND FOR WHICH CATEGORIES: UNVERIFIED — this needs a market-by-market enquiry, not an assumption of uniformity.
subdivisions.authority: Directive (EU) 2015/849 (AMLD4) Art 2(2); equivalent option preserved in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 / the AML package — exact AMLR article UNVERIFIED

subdivisions.name: [AUDIT ADDITION] All 27 member states — European Accessibility Act national enforcement
subdivisions.detail: [AUDIT ADDITION]. Directive (EU) 2019/882 requirements have APPLIED since 28 June 2025 and expressly cover e-commerce and consumer-facing digital services — websites and mobile apps used to conclude consumer contracts, i.e. your coin shop and subscription checkout. Art 4(5) exempts microenterprises PROVIDING SERVICES, which is the only reason FACT//DUEL can ignore it today; the exemption falls away at 10 staff or EUR 2m turnover. Enforcement is by NATIONAL market surveillance authorities with national penalty regimes, so the practical exposure varies by market and the specific national penalty provisions are UNVERIFIED. Design the checkout and the timer/motion/audio-cue vocabulary to accessibility standards now: retrofitting a juice-heavy, timer-driven game UI later is materially more expensive than building it in.
subdivisions.authority: Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) Arts 2, 4(5) — applicable 28 June 2025; national transpositions and market surveillance authorities — specific provisions UNVERIFIED

risks: [CORRECTED] TRANSFERABILITY, NOT REDEEMABILITY, IS THE E-MONEY CLIFF EDGE. The original brief warned that a goodwill cash refund or an account-closure return of an unspent balance could convert you into an unauthorised e-money issuer. That is WRONG and the advice was actively harmful: EMD2 Art 2(2) limb (ii) requires acceptance by a person OTHER THAN the issuer, and a refund paid by you to your own customer involves no third party accepting anything — nor does an account-closure balance return, nor the statutory CRD withdrawal refund this brief itself mandates. Consumer-friendly refunds are lawful and partly compulsory; do not suppress them on a mistaken legal basis. THE REAL LIMB-(ii) RISKS are: player-to-player coin gifting or trading, a tournament that pays winners in transferable coins, any third-party merchant accepting your coin, and any grey market that can price the balance. Write the NO-TRANSFER, NO-THIRD-PARTY-ACCEPTANCE rule into the product spec and the terms, and make it a code-level invariant with a test.

[CORRECTED] AML IS LIVE TODAY FOR MODEL B AND POSSIBLY MODEL C — NOT FROM 10 JULY 2027. This was the most dangerous framing in the original brief. AMLD4 Art 2(1)(3)(f) has made providers of gambling services obliged entities EU-wide since the 26 June 2017 transposition deadline, and AMLD4 Art 3(14) already carries the 'games of chance, including those with an element of skill' definition. A Model B launch in late 2026 built to a 2027 AML start date would be operating unlawfully in most member states on day one: no CDD, no transaction monitoring, no FIU reporting, no registration with the national AML supervisor. CDD bites at EUR 2,000 on collection of winnings, wagering of a stake, or both, single or linked (AMLD4 Art 11(d); AMLR Art 19). Comply with national AML law NOW; re-paper to the AMLR by 10 July 2027.

[CORRECTED] THE AMLR DOES NOT END PER-MARKET DIVERGENCE. AMLD4 Art 2(2) lets member states exempt certain gambling services (not casinos) on proven low risk with notification to the Commission, and the AML package preserves an equivalent option. So 'it is a regulation, therefore uniform' is false in the one respect that matters: whether YOU are an obliged entity remains a 27-market question after 10 July 2027. This cuts both ways — it is also the most plausible escape hatch for Model C, and the original brief omitted it.

[CORRECTED] MODEL C'S VAT TREATMENT IS NOT SETTLED. The original brief called the entry fee 'settled' as a taxable electronically supplied service after testing only Art 135(1)(e). Art 135(1)(i) exempts betting, lotteries and other forms of gambling subject to each member state's conditions and limitations. If a state characterises the paid-entry duel as gambling — the same question the brief calls unresolved for AML — the fee may be VAT-EXEMPT there, outside your OSS return, with input-VAT recovery consequences. For any staked leg, the Glawe line (C-38/93; C-377/11) can make the taxable amount the operator's retained margin rather than gross stakes. Both change the revenue model materially and both were missing.

[CORRECTED] C-472/24 IS NARROWER THAN THE BRIEF CLAIMED, AND YOUR VAT OBLIGATION DOES NOT DEPEND ON IT. The taxable person in MB 'Zaidimu valiuta' was a THIRD-PARTY TRADER reselling RuneScape gold on a secondary market, not a publisher issuing its own currency, and the single-purpose voucher question under Art 30a(2) for a first-party issuer was never before the Court. Extending the holding to your own coin sale is a reasonable inference, not law. The good news: it does not matter much, because the obligation to charge destination VAT from the first euro follows from Art 58 plus the fact that the Art 59c EUR 10,000 threshold applies only to EU-established sellers. Take the conservative position; document it as an inference; do not cite the case as though it decided your facts.

VAT IS OWED AT THE COIN SALE, NOT AT THE SPEND — AND THIS BREAKS NAIVE FINANCIAL MODELS. On the conservative reading you owe destination-country VAT on the full consideration the moment coins are bought, before the player has consumed anything. Combined with the (contested) CPC position that unspent coins remain refundable for 14 days, you can be liable for VAT on a sale you later have to reverse. Model the cash-flow and build VAT-credit handling into the refund path.

THE 14-DAY UNSPENT-COIN REFUND POSITION IS A FRAUD VECTOR IN A STAKING GAME. If a player can buy coins, stake and lose them, and then demand a refund, you have built a free-roll. The CPC position limits the right to UNSPENT currency, so the mitigation is a strict FIFO lot ledger that marks coins consumed at the moment of stake, plus clear disclosure. Get this architecture right before launch; it is close to impossible to retrofit onto a balance-only ledger.

[RE-LABELLED] THE CPC KEY PRINCIPLES ARE SOFT LAW AND PARTS OF THEM ARE GENUINELY CONTESTED — THE ORIGINAL HEADLINE CALLED THEM 'NON-NEGOTIABLE'. Footnote 1 of the document states it 'does therefore by no means bind the national authorities or the European Commission' and that non-compliance is not necessarily unlawful. Video Games Europe and the EGDF have publicly said the Network introduced new legal theories; German courts have upheld properly-constructed withdrawal-right waivers for virtual currency. Two of the original brief's 'four hard obligations' — the unspent-coin refund right and the real-money price display — rest wholly on this document. You could win the argument. But the Principles state the enforcement posture of the authorities who would open the file, and a CPC coordinated action is itself the punishment. Build to them; book them as posture, not as law.

DESIGNING FOR WHALES IS EXPRESSLY A CONSUMER-LAW RISK, NOT JUST AN ETHICS QUESTION. The CPC Key Principles treat high-spending players as a VULNERABLE group likely to struggle with impulse control or gambling disorders, and say a business model based on targeting them is assessed under a stricter fairness threshold under UCPD Arts 5-9. FACT//DUEL's existing juice, streak, escrow and ceremony vocabulary is exactly the design language this is aimed at. A monetisation plan built on whale extraction is a UCPD exposure regardless of which model you pick.

YOU WILL BE DEEMED TO HAVE CHILD PLAYERS WHETHER YOU TARGET THEM OR NOT. The CPC Network states that any game not exclusively intended for adults should expect a significant under-18 player base, and that age gates do not discharge the trader's responsibility. A trivia game is the archetype of a product children reach. This drives the DPIA requirement, the Art 8 GDPR parental-consent gate, the spending-off-by-default expectation, and the UCPD Annex I point 28 ban on direct exhortation — which is hard law in the directive itself and needs no CPC theory. All of it applies to Model A too.

[AUDIT ADDITION] CRD ART 8(2) NON-COMPLIANCE IS REVENUE REVERSAL, NOT A FINE. If the coin-purchase button is not labelled to make the payment obligation unambiguous and the consumer is not made to acknowledge it explicitly, THE CONSUMER IS NOT BOUND BY THE CONTRACT. This applies to every coin-purchase surface in Models A, B and C, not just a subscription confirm. It is the cheapest fix in this document and the most expensive omission.

[AUDIT ADDITION] A US- OR OFFSHORE-LAW ToS DOES NOT SOLVE THE EU. Rome I Art 6(1)-(2) applies the mandatory consumer-protection law of the consumer's habitual residence to a trader directing activities to that member state, and a choice-of-law clause cannot deprive the consumer of it; Brussels Ia Art 18 lets them sue at home. A founder handed a US template may believe the governing-law clause disposes of the CRD, UCPD, UCTD and DCD. It does not. Assume 27 sets of mandatory rules apply to everything that cannot be contracted away.

[AUDIT ADDITION] COLLECTIVE REDRESS IS THE REALISTIC ENFORCEMENT VECTOR AND THE ORIGINAL BRIEF NEVER MENTIONED IT. Directive (EU) 2020/1828 on representative actions has applied since 25 June 2023: qualified entities can bring cross-border collective redress for infringements of the CRD, UCPD, UCTD, DCD and the GDPR. For a coin economy that will demonstrably reach minors, a qualified-entity action is at least as likely as a regulator action and carries damages rather than commitments.

[AUDIT ADDITION] DIRECTIVE (EU) 2019/770 ART 19 IS THE HARD LIMIT ON REBALANCING A PAID COIN ECONOMY. The original brief attributed this constraint to UCTD Art 3 and the CPC Principles alone. DCD Art 19 is hard law: modification of a continuously-supplied digital service requires a contractual basis, a valid reason, no extra cost and advance notice on a durable medium, and where the change adversely affects access or use the consumer may TERMINATE FREE and claim reimbursement under Arts 16-18. Design the economy on the assumption that you cannot devalue or withdraw what people paid for.

[AUDIT ADDITION] THE EUROPEAN ACCESSIBILITY ACT IS A DELAYED-FUSE COST. Directive (EU) 2019/882 has applied since 28 June 2025 to consumer-facing e-commerce services. You are exempt only as a microenterprise service provider (Art 4(5)); the exemption evaporates at 10 staff or EUR 2m turnover — i.e. exactly when a monetised launch succeeds. Retrofitting WCAG-level accessibility into a timer-driven, heavily animated, audio-cued game is expensive. Build the checkout accessibly now.

[CORRECTED] THE EU-US DATA PRIVACY FRAMEWORK COULD FALL AGAIN MID-BUILD. It is valid today. The General Court dismissed the challenge in Case T-553/23 Latombe v Commission on 3 September 2025; the appeal was lodged 31 October 2025 and is pending as Case C-703/25 P (case number corroborated by independent sources and retained). The original brief's additional claims of 'no hearing date announced as at mid-2026' and 'Microsoft granted leave to intervene on 29 June 2026' are UNCORROBORATED and removed. The CJEU killed both predecessor frameworks. Do not design a US-processor architecture with no fallback: SCCs plus transfer impact assessments in every US vendor contract NOW, and know which processors you could move to EU regions.

[CORRECTED] PSD3/PSR WILL RESHUFFLE THE PERIMETER RIGHT AFTER YOU LAUNCH — AND IT REPEALS EMD2. Provisional political agreement 27 November 2025 is corroborated; the brief's '23 April 2026 final compromise texts' date is not, and is removed. The cited source puts expected OJ publication at end of Q2 2026 and PSR application at 18 months after entry into force (payee-name verification at 24), not ~21 months. MATERIAL AND PREVIOUSLY OMITTED: PSD3 REPEALS EMD2 OUTRIGHT; existing EMI authorisations survive only 24 months after entry into force (extendable to 30) with a MANDATORY RE-APPLICATION. So an EMI licence obtained for Model B in 2027 would need re-papering almost immediately. Build Model B only with counsel tracking the PSR text.

BETAAL GARANT IS A THINNER SHIELD THAN IT LOOKS. C-51/25 (16 July 2026) is genuinely helpful — ancillary fund transfers serving a primary non-payment service are outside PSD2 — but practitioners describe it as fact-specific and confined, it turned partly on the intermediary not holding the payer's payment account, it did NOT address money remittance, and further CJEU references are pending. Holding named per-player balances is the fact most likely to defeat the ancillary argument. Do not let anyone treat this judgment as a licence substitute.

THE DIGITAL FAIRNESS ACT IS A KNOWN FUTURE RESET AND EVERY TIMELINE CLAIM ABOUT IT IS PRESS REPORTING. A proposal expected H2 2026 covering dark patterns, addictive design, loot boxes and virtual currencies will land on this exact product category. The cheap insurance is to build the real-money price display, the exact-amount coin purchase and the no-randomised-paid-rewards rule now, so the DFA is a documentation exercise rather than a rebuild.

A SINGLE FEATURE CAN FLIP YOU INTO THE FULL DSA ONLINE-PLATFORM REGIME. Today you are probably not even an intermediary; with accounts you are probably a hosting service (Arts 11, 12, 14, 16 — NOT Art 15, which Art 15(2) disapplies for micro/small enterprises); with public leaderboards carrying user-authored text, global chat, or user-generated question packs you become an 'online platform' and acquire Arts 20-28, including the Art 28 minor-protection duty. Put a DSA scoping gate in the product review process for any social feature.

[CONTESTED] THE AI ACT OMNIBUS DATES IN THE ORIGINAL BRIEF ARE UNCORROBORATED. The claim that the AI Omnibus was 'adopted by Council 29 June 2026, published in the OJ 24 July 2026 and entered into force 27 July 2026' matches no reachable source; the brief's own citation records only political agreement 6 May 2026 and Council confirmation 13 May 2026, with adoption and OJ publication 'expected before 2 August 2026'. Treat the dates as contested and verify the OJ citation before relying on any deferral. The substance holds: Annex III stand-alone high-risk deferred to 2 December 2027, Annex I embedded high-risk to 2 August 2028, Art 5 prohibitions NOT deferred and in force since 2 February 2025, Art 50 transparency obligations live from 2 August 2026, and a new Art 5 prohibition (nudifiers/CSAM) added with a transitional period to 2 December 2026.

TODAY'S DEMO COINS ARE OUTSIDE ALL OF THIS — AND THAT IS A ONE-WAY DOOR. Footnote 2 of the CPC Key Principles expressly excludes in-game currencies obtainable solely through gameplay and not purchasable with real-world money. FACT//DUEL's current demo coins and Expedition points sit in that carve-out. The moment a purchase path exists, the entire consumer-law layer switches on for the design, not just for the new purchase flow — including the price-display and no-stacked-currency principles that constrain how points and coins may relate to each other.

WHETHER A TIMED TRIVIA DUEL IS A 'GAME OF CHANCE WITH AN ELEMENT OF SKILL': genuinely open, and — corrected — this is a PRESENT-TENSE question under AMLD4 Art 3(14), not a 2027 question under the AMLR. No case law, no guidance. It is the single largest unresolved question for Models B and C, and it simultaneously determines gambling licensing, AML obliged-entity status, and VAT Art 135(1)(i) exemption.

corrections: [CERTAIN] HEADLINE REWRITTEN. The e-money cliff edge is NOT redeemability. EMD2 Art 2(2) has no redeemability limb; its two cumulative elements are (i) stored monetary value representing a claim on the issuer, issued on receipt of funds for the purpose of making payment transactions, and (ii) acceptance by a person OTHER THAN the issuer. EBA Q&A 2022_6336 (Final, 17/01/2025, citing CJEU C-661/22) reads limb (ii) as requiring transferability and voluntary acceptance of the instrument as a separate monetary asset. Art 11 redemption at par is a consequence of being an issuer, not a trigger. Corrected test: THIRD-PARTY ACCEPTANCE AND TRANSFERABILITY, with redeemability as evidence of payment purpose under limb (i).

[CERTAIN] RISK REGISTER CORRECTED: a goodwill cash refund, an account-closure return of an unspent balance, and the statutory CRD withdrawal refund CANNOT satisfy EMD2 limb (ii), because no third party accepts the coin — the payment runs from issuer back to its own customer. The original brief's advice to avoid consumer-friendly refunds on this basis was wrong and is removed. Only the player-to-player transfer / grey-market limb of that sentence survives, and it has been promoted to the primary risk.

[CERTAIN] THE AMLR DID NOT GIVE THE FIRST EU-WIDE DEFINITION OF 'GAMBLING SERVICE'. Directive (EU) 2015/849 (AMLD4) Art 3(14) already defines it in materially identical words and has been EU law since the 26 June 2017 transposition deadline. The AMLR carries the wording into a regulation; it does not invent it.

[CERTAIN] AML IS LIVE NOW, NOT FROM 10 JULY 2027. AMLD4 Art 2(1)(3)(f) has made providers of gambling services obliged entities EU-wide since 2017 under national transpositions — CDD, transaction monitoring, FIU reporting, registration with the national AML supervisor. The checklist item was rewritten from 'build AML/CFT capability for a 10 July 2027 start date' to 'comply with national AML law NOW; re-paper to the AMLR by 10 July 2027'. This was the single most dangerous framing in the original brief: a Model B launch in late 2026 built to the 2027 date would have been unlawful in most member states on day one.

[CERTAIN] DSA ART 15 REMOVED FROM THE BASELINE DUTIES. Art 15(2) disapplies transparency reporting for providers that are micro or small enterprises under Recommendation 2003/361/EC and are not VLOPs under Art 33. The brief assumes micro/small status elsewhere (it relies on Art 19 for exactly that), so listing Art 15 as a size-blind duty was a misstatement generating unnecessary annual reporting work. Arts 11, 12, 14 and 16 are retained.

[CERTAIN] MODEL C'S VAT TREATMENT DE-SETTLED. The brief tested only Art 135(1)(e). Art 135(1)(i) exempts betting, lotteries and other forms of gambling subject to each member state's conditions and limitations, so a state that characterises the paid-entry duel as gambling may treat the fee as VAT-exempt and outside OSS, with input-VAT consequences. The Glawe line (C-38/93; C-377/11 International Bingo Technology), which can make the taxable amount the operator's retained margin, was also missing and is added. A new checklist item captures both.

[CERTAIN] THE 'FOUR NON-NEGOTIABLE / HARD OBLIGATIONS' FRAMING RE-LABELLED. Two of the four — the unspent-coin refund right and real-money price labelling — rest wholly on the CPC Key Principles, whose footnote 1 states the document 'does therefore by no means bind the national authorities or the European Commission' and that non-compliance is not necessarily unlawful. Video Games Europe and EGDF dispute the 'virtual currency is not digital content' premise and German courts have gone the other way. Now presented as declared ENFORCEMENT POSTURE (still worth building to) rather than as obligations. The two genuinely hard ones — destination VAT and the CRD information/button/withdrawal package — are retained as obligations.
